chain.g: dust, dried earth reduced to powder; other dry material reduced to powder

ety.text: From Middle English dust, doust, from Old English dūst (“dust, dried earth reduced to powder; other dry material reduced to powder”), from the fusion of Proto-Germanic *dustą (“dust”) and *dunstą (“mist, dust, evaporation”), both from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust”). Cognate with Scots dust, dist (“dust”), Dutch duist (“pollen, dust”) and dons (“down, fuzz”), German Dust (“dust”) and Dunst (“haze”), Swedish dust (“dust”), Icelandic dust (“dust”), Latin fūmus (“smoke, steam”). Also related to Swedish dun (“down, fluff”), Icelandic dúnn (“down, fluff”). See down.

senses.d: Fine, dry particles of matter found in the air and covering the surface of objects, typically consisting of soil lifted up by the wind, pollen, hair, fiber debris, dead skin cells, etc.
ex: There is so much dust released during the process of laying ballast that the trackside operator wears a full face mask with respirator.

senses.d: Any substance reduced to fine particles; powder.
Submicron particles in outer space, largely silicates and carbon compounds, that contribute greatly to extinction at visible wavelengths.
ex: Astronomers have previously considered that dust produced by the star was obscuring it, causing the steep decline in brightness.

senses.d: Disintegration of a solid, like silica.
Flour.
A single fine, dry particle of earth or other material; grain of dust.
ex: to touch a dust of England’s ground

senses.d: The act of cleaning by dusting.
ex: […]once they start school, I mean you can do a room out one day, the next day it only needs a dust, doesn’t it?

senses.d: The act of sprinkling dust, or a sprinkle of dust itself.
Earth, ground, soil, sediment.
The earth as the resting place of the dead.
ex: For now shall I sleep in the dust.

senses.d: To remove dust from.
ex: The cleaning lady needs a stool to dust the cupboard.

senses.d: To remove dust; to clean by removing dust.
ex: Dusting always makes me cough.

senses.d: To make dusty, to soil with dust.
Of a bird, to cover itself in sand or dry, dusty earth.
To spray or cover (something) with fine powder or liquid, to sprinkle.
ex: The mother dusted her baby’s bum with talcum powder.

senses.d: To sprinkle (a substance) in the form of dust.
To leave quickly; to rush off.
ex: He added in a casual tone: ‘The girl can dust. I’d like to talk to you a little, soldier.’

senses.d: To drink up quickly; to toss off.
To reduce to a fine powder; to pulverize, to levigate.
ex: good Powder differs from bad […]in having more Peter and less Coal; and lastly, in the well dusting of it

senses.d: To strike, beat, thrash.

grp.label: to spray something with fine powder or liquid

ety.text: Inherited from Old French pousiere, derived from pous, from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, neuter form derived from Latin pulvis m.
Inherited from Latin pulverem, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”). Doublet of polve, from the Latin nominative pulvis. Akin to Sicilian prùvula.

es:polvo.gl: dust (fine, dry particles of matter found in the air and covering the surface of objects)

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *pel-der. Latin pulvisder. Vulgar Latin *pulvus Old Spanish polvos Spanish polvo Inherited from Old Spanish polvos (singular), from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, neuter form derived from Classical Latin pulvis m, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Compare English pulverise.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese poo, from Vulgar Latin *pulus, from earlier *pulvus n, from Latin pulvis m, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“flour, dust”). Compare Galician po, Spanish polvo.

pt:poeira.gl: dust (fine, dry particles in the air or covering objects)

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old Spanish des- Spanish des- Spanish empolvar Spanish desempolvar From des- + empolvar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pulverizāre, from Latin pulvis, pulveris (“dust, powder”) (whence French poudre).
From es- + polvo (“powder”) + -ear, or es- + polvorear.
From Middle English dusty, dusti, from Old English dūstiġ, dystiġ, dȳstiġ (“dusty”), equivalent to dust + -y. Cognate with Dutch donzig (“cottony, downy, woolly”), German dunstig (“hazy, misty”).

senses.d: Covered with dust.
ex: a dusty carpet
On a cold morning in Abilene, Texas, a column of 18-wheelers crawls down bumpy, waterlogged roads, past cattle grazing on dusty shrubs.

senses.d: Powdery and resembling dust.
Grey or greyish.
ex: a dusty peach color

senses.d: Old; outdated; stuffily traditional.
Ugly, disgusting (a general term of abuse).
Ugly, unwell, inadequate, bad.
ex: One morning, I said to a patient: "How are you today, Mrs. White?" And she replied "Not so dusty - quite well brushed."
"Never mind," she ventured, "but thanks for the compliment. You're not so dusty yourself!"

senses.d: A medium-brown color.
An old bottle of spirits that has been kept for a long time.
ex: A lighter, less expensive version—The White Label—was taken off the market in 2016. But dusties can still be found.

senses.d: A miller (from the image of millers being covered in flour dust).
ex: I do not like to see too much strife between dusties on the short and long system question, as it is liable to cause hard feelings.
It is designed to do scalping and grading in a way to satiffy the most fastidious of dusties.

senses.d: A supply petty officer.
ex: From time to time I'd get up to the dusties' mess for this or that reason, and became known to the writers and dusties up there.
Take the Jack Dusties, the stores blokes, they were in our mess.

senses.d: A recording of music from another era, especially R&B; an oldie.
ex: In Los Angeles, listeners can tune in to KACE, the "dusties" station that plays music from the '50s, '60s and '70s;
WGCI 1390 - AM was previously known for playing R & B oldies known as "dusties".

senses.d: An old person, especially one who is unwilling to change with the times.
A person of mixed race who has a swarthy complexion.
ex: Ashy niggas and dusties went everywhere, forgetting about looking dap.

senses.d: A migrant farmer from the dustbowl.
A dustman.
A duststorm.
